newsitem.title: JAPAN: Rubin urges Japan not to let trade surplus surge.
newsitem.headline: Rubin urges Japan not to let trade surplus surge.

text.p: U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin urged Japan on Friday to guard against a resurgence of its trade surplus, but rejected suggestions that a stronger Japanese currency was the best way to do that.

In a speech for delivery to the American Chamber of Commerce in Japan, Rubin said Japan needed to promote strong domestic demand for its products, open up its markets further to imports and deregulate its economy.

It is critical that Japan's current account surplus not rise again to a level that is detrimental to global growth, that causes trade friction with Japan's trading partners and that could fuel protectionist sentiments, he said in his speech after meeting Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto.
Japan's trade surplus rose in February for the first time in two years, as the weak Japanese yen helped make the nation's exports more competitive in world markets.
Speaking to reporters on his way here, Rubin made clear that he did not see a stronger yen -- and by inference a weaker dollar -- as the best way to contain and cut Japan's surplus.
We don't believe in anybody using their currency for trade policies -- us or anybody else, he said.
Rubin acknowledged that trade balances tend to fluctuate. But he told the business executives that Japan needed to avoid a significant increase in its surplus by promoting strong domestic demand.

Some U.S. officials are particularly worried about Tokyo's plan to sharply tighten budget policy, fearing that a rise in consumption taxes that took effect this week will sap demand at home and force Japanese companies to look abroad for sales.
Rubin told reporters ahead of the meeting with Hashimoto that he might discuss the budget with the prime minister, but added that he did not intend to make any specific policy prescriptions.
In his speech, Rubin urged Japan to press ahead with its efforts to shore up its banking system, warning that any delay would only increase the costs of resolving the problem.
Japanese banks are saddled with billions of dollars in bad loans, a legacy of the collapse of the property market after the asset bubble of the late 1980's.
Rubin also called on Tokyo to follow through on Hashimoto's promise of deregulation. The faster these reforms are put in place, the better, he said.
Looking back over the past four years, Rubin said that both the United States and Japan had worked hard to iron out trade friction and strengthen their economic relationship.
He noted that Japan's current account surplus -- the broadest measure of trade -- has fallen from the equivalent of 3.1 percent of gross domestic product in 1993 to 1.4 percent.
A few years ago, Washington unsuccessfully tried to convince Tokyo to adopt a surplus target of one-and-a-half to two percent of gross domestic product.
Rubin told reporters that was not necessarily pertinent now but said he was not advocating eliminating the surplus.
The Treasury chief's visit comes on the heels of trips to Tokyo by U.S. Vice President Al Gore and Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers.
Rubin denied that this represented a concerted U,S. strategy to turn up the heat on Japan.

Rubin was scheduled to meet Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka at noon (0300 GMT) before holding a news conference ahead of his departure for the Philippines for a meeting of Asia-Pacific finance ministers.
